sentences.text: Its skull featured a slightly bent jugal bone creating a curved margin below the eye socket, while the bone was notably narrow compared to other relatives.
Additionally, the atlas and axis vertebrae were fused together, though a visible suture line remained.
The jaws held approximately 152 long, needle-like teeth that were tightly packed and projected outward.
In each jaw, the first tooth was about half the length of the second tooth.
When the jaws closed, these interlocking teeth formed a comb-like structure designed for filter-feeding.
The genus Liaodactylus was described by Zhou et al. in 2017.
Only one specimen is known, the holotype PMOL-AP00031, which is housed at the Palaeontological Museum of Liaoning.
Liaodactylus is classified as a filter-feeding ctenochasmatid pterosaur from the Jurassic of China.
Zhou and colleagues assigned the animal to the family Ctenochasmatidae in 2017 based on a phylogenetic analysis.
Phylogenetic analysis places Liaodactylus closest to Ctenochasma, sharing similar jaw-to-skull ratios and outward-angled teeth.
The animal inhabited a forested woodland environment containing conifers, cycads, and ferns.
The climate where it lived was cool, temperate, wet, and seasonal, with a mean temperature below 15 °C.

Liaodactylus is known from the Tiaojishan Formation, which along with the older Haifanggou Formation forms the Yanliao biota, a diverse and well-preserved association of Jurassic animals containing at least 40 species, though a 2023 study proposed that the fossils belong to the Haifanggou Formation rather than the Tiaojishan Formation.
